paras: The lynching near Coushatta, Louisiana, was the hanging of an unidentified Black man by a mob of armed men early on Saturday, August 21, 1915, after he was accused of entering the bedroom of a farmer's 17-year-old daughter and trying to assault her. The mob took the man from a deputy sheriff who had him in custody and hanged him in a nearby swamp. The killing was reported in brief wire items in white newspapers from Alabama to Idaho over the following week.

The young woman was the daughter of Ed or Edward Adcock, described in one dispatch as "a well-known farmer" and in another as "a planter living near Coushatta." According to the fullest wire account, she discovered a man in her room after she had gone to bed, fought him off, and gave the alarm.

Accounts differ on how the man was caught. The Associated Press version said neighbors caught him a few minutes later and turned him over to a deputy sheriff, while a Shreveport dispatch said Deputy Sheriff Scott captured him himself "after a short chase." Before the deputy could get him to jail, a mob formed, overpowered the officer, and forced him to give up his prisoner.

The mob, described as "a body of armed men," hanged the man in a swamp near the farm, which the Shreveport dispatch identified as Grand Bayou swamp. None of the reports gave his name, and all called him only "an unidentified negro" or "an unknown negro."
No report of an inquest, arrests, or any official inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage.

The story moved over the Associated Press wire under a dateline printed variously as "COUSHAMA," "COUSHANA" and "Couchama," while the Shreveport dispatch named the place as Coushatta. The Montgomery Advertiser and the Clarksburg Sunday Telegram printed the wire on August 22, and the Washington Times ran the Shreveport version on its front page the same day. The Omaha Daily Bee carried it on August 23, and the Tulsa Daily World and The Farmer and Mechanic followed on August 24. Weeklies picked it up later in the week: the Batesville Guard in Arkansas reprinted the Tulsa text on August 25 and 27 under the head "Mob Takes Quick Action," the Butler Weekly Times in Missouri ran the Shreveport version on August 26, and the Bonners Ferry Herald in Idaho reduced it to one garbled line in a world-news summary on August 27.

Several headlines presented the accusation as established fact, among them the Washington Times's "Mob Lynches Negro Who Broke Into Girl's Room" and the Omaha Daily Bee's "Negro Attacks Girl; Lynched by a Mob." The Tulsa Daily World headed its story "NEGRO ASSAILANT LYNCHED BY MOB" and added that he "Was Dealt Summarily With" before officers arrived, although its own text said a deputy already had him in custody when the mob took him. The shortest Associated Press items, by contrast, called the man "accused," and only The Farmer and Mechanic's version said the young woman was white. No account of the lynching in the Black press appears in the coverage.

The dispatches differ slightly on the date: copies datelined August 21 said the lynching happened "early today" or "early Saturday morning," while the Omaha Daily Bee's copy, datelined August 22, said it happened "today." They also differ on the accusation itself: the Shreveport dispatch said only that the man "entered the bed room" of the young woman, while the wire spoke of an attempt to "attack" or "assault" her. Every version of the accusation came from the accusers' side, and none of the reports recorded anything the man himself said.
